NASA POWER · MERRA-2 1991–2025

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

Is the trend in the planet, or in the sample?

We tested 80 climate trends in NASA reanalysis data, corrected for false discoveries, then audited our own best story. It didn’t survive. This tool shows why.

01 · One place

while its rain rose.

A striking pair of trends in 35 years of MERRA-2. It is the kind of result that becomes a headline: more rain, cooler air. So we asked whether it holds anywhere else.

03 · The audit

Then we audited ourselves.

—
Spearman ρ, rainfall trend against temperature trend

On the 12 sites we picked, wetter places cooled. On 28 grid points nobody picked, the relationship vanishes. The pattern was in our sample, not the planet.

Method & credits

Method

Annual values from NASA POWER monthly point data (MERRA-2 reanalysis), 1991–2025. Trend by Mann–Kendall (two-sided, tie-corrected) and Sen's slope, computed in ingest.py. Multiple comparisons controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg. A significant trend is evidence of a change, not an explanation of one: reanalysis grid cells are modelled estimates, not thermometers, and 35 years is short for separating a trend from a multi-decade cycle.

Data & credits

NASA POWER monthly point API (MERRA-2, community AG) · T2M, PRECTOTCORR. Globe imagery: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble (NASA Earth Observatory). Map outline: Natural Earth 1:110m (public domain). Methods: Mann (1945); Kendall (1975); Sen (1968); Benjamini & Hochberg (1995).

NASA and the NASA Space Apps Challenge logo are official event branding, used unmodified for challenge identification only. Challenge: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

Use of AI — disclosure

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Fast was used under the team's direction and review for the analysis pipeline, ingest.py, the web demo and first drafts of the writeup. Every number on this page is produced by running that committed code on public data; no figure, statistic or claim is generated by a language model. The statistical choices (Mann–Kendall, Sen's slope, Benjamini–Hochberg) are standard published methods, cited below, selected and reviewed by the team.
